newsitem.title: UK: English Church homosexuality debate inconclusive.
newsitem.headline: English Church homosexuality debate inconclusive.

text.p: The governing body of the Church of England has passed a motion keeping the door open for further debate on regulations banning actively homosexual priests.

Hymn-singing gay activists outside the synod meeting welcomed the decision and brandished a banner saying "One small step forward", but at least one gay campaigner acknowledged the ambiguousness of the move.
"It's not exactly revolutionary," the activist said.

The motion moved on Monday by London Archdeacon David Gerrard urged church members to acknowledge that a 1991 bishops' report which sanctioned gay relationships for the laity but not for the clergy was "not the last word on the subject".

It coincided with a move by Britain's new Labour government towards lowering the age of consent for homosexuals from 18 to 16 by saying it would not contest a case before the European Court of Human Rights. . Archbishop of Canterbury George Carey, the spiritual leader of the church whose head is Queen Elizabeth, made clear in a speech that the church was far from accepting actively homosexual clergy.

"I do not find any justification, from the Bible or the entire Christian tradition, for sexual activity outside marriage. Thus, same sex relationships in my view cannot be on a par with marriage," Carey said.
Although the decision was welcomed by gay activists, some delegates at the annual synod in York, northern England, pointed out that discussion could also lead to a hardening of the present position.

Some 25 protestors from the Lesbian and Gay Christian Movement (LGCM) and the Action for Gay and Lesbian Ordination group (AGLO) mounted a day-long vigil outside the synod, wielding banners saying "Fear not --speak out" and singing traditional hymns adapted to gay themes.

The Reverend Richard Kirker, general secretary of the Lesbian and Gay Christian Movement, said: "We feel it is a good result. The fact that people did not vote for the proposed amendments shows they do not agree with Carey."
The church, which has some 80 million members worldwide, has long been accused of hypocrisy in its policy towards homosexual clergy.

A survey published by the LGCM on Sunday said at least 37 British bishops, some now dead or retired, had knowingly ordained, licensed or employed actively gay priests, despite the church's teaching to the contrary.

A vote by a division -- members filing through certain doors according to their voting choice -- resulted in a clear majority for the motion, but showed the issue was one which has sharply divided the Church of England.

Several members of the clergy said if gay priests were openly accepted the numbers of both clergy and lay people who would leave as a result would far outnumber those who left after the 1992 synod decision to ordain women priests.
One lay speaker said: "Homosexuals have a choice. They are not born as such and the choice to go on sinning is theirs."
She said homosexuality was "an insidious, but deadly erosion of God's standard of living."
This was the first time the issue of homosexuality had been debated at a synod since 1987, when it was voted that "homosexual acts fall short of (God's) ideal".
